title: Free speech and equal rights
hookLine: from Severus: the idea of a state with equal law and free speech (Meditations 1.14)

cards: Here's a sentence from an unlikely pen.

A man with an army, the final say in law, and the power of life and death over an empire writes in his private notebook that he's grateful someone taught him the idea of a state where the same law applies to everyone, where people have an equal right to speak, and where the ruler respects, above all, the freedom of the ruled.

teach.b: First, Severus. Marcus calls him my brother. He's probably Claudius Severus, a philosopher whose son married one of Marcus's daughters, so brother may be a family word, not a literal one.
From him, Marcus says, he learned to love his family, truth and justice. Second, the heroes.
Through Severus, Marcus came to know about Cato and Brutus, from the last days of the Roman Republic, and Thrasea and Helvidius, senators who stood up to emperors and were killed or exiled for it.
An heir to the throne, learning to admire people who defied the throne. Third, the idea.

From Severus, Marcus says, he received the idea of a state with one law for all, run on equal rights and equal freedom of speech, and of a monarchy that respects most of all the freedom of the governed.
The same entry adds that Severus said plainly what he disapproved of, so his friends never had to guess. Fourth, honesty about Rome.
Marcus's empire was not that state. Rome held slaves, and its law did not treat the powerful and the poor alike. Historians still argue about how far Marcus lived up to the idea.
But the entry shows a ruler who kept, in his private notes, a picture of something better than the system he ran, and named the man who gave it to him.
Equal voices start small. Not in a senate. At a table, when someone you disagree with is speaking, and you let them finish.

how: Readers who take this entry seriously often practice letting people they disagree with finish speaking, and say their own disagreements openly rather than hiding them.

o: a senator killed for standing up to a cruel emperor
the teacher who gave Marcus the idea of equal free speech
the general who took the throne after Marcus died

games.q: free speech and equal rights — tap the pairs.
p: senators who stood up to emperors
respects the freedom of the ruled

s: Marcus's Rome treated everyone equally under the law
Rome held slaves, and its law did not treat the powerful and the poor alike.
through Severus, Marcus learned to admire people who defied emperors
Severus hid his disapproval so his friends never knew where they stood
Marcus says his friends never had to guess his views.

games.q: you're the heir to Rome's throne. a friend tells you about senators who defied emperors and paid for it. what do you do with that?
o: admire them, and keep the idea of equal law and free speech.
make sure no one like them ever rises again.
games.why: Marcus thanks Severus for teaching him about them, and for the idea of a state with equal law and freedom of speech.

practice: Bring to mind an opinion you really dislike, held by someone real, and picture them saying it; notice the urge to interrupt or scroll past.
In your mind, let them finish, all the way, then ask one honest question: what might they be afraid of, or hoping for? You don't have to agree.

wordCard.voice: Severus. The philosopher from whom Marcus took the idea of a state with one law for all, equal speech, and rulers who respect the freedom of the ruled. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: equal right to speak, an old Athenian ideal. Marcus uses it of the state Severus described.

carryVoice: Your line: equal voices. An emperor kept that picture in his private notes. That's day five hundred twenty-eight.
